title: Teaching, Supervising & & Knowledge Exchange
text: I support the development of early-career researchers, and strengthen their expertise in epidemiology, animal and public health. Across university teaching, postgraduate supervision, professional training, and specialist residency programmes, I aim to equip students and professionals with the analytical skills, critical thinking, and scientific independence needed to address complex animal and public health challenges.

title: Teaching, Supervising & & Knowledge Exchange
text:
University Teaching and Academic Supervision
In 2024–2025, I served as Associate Professor of Statistics at Universidad Alfonso X el Sabio (UAX), teaching foundational and applied statistics to Veterinary Medicine students. My teaching connected statistical principles with practical applications in veterinary science, helping students develop the quantitative skills needed to interpret data and support evidence-based decisions.
My university supervision experience includes directing an MSc thesis at the Universidad Alfonso X el Sabio (UAX), entitled “Análisis epidemiológico de la dermatitis nodular contagiosa en Europa” (2025–2026). I support students throughout the research process, from formulating research questions and designing studies to managing data, conducting epidemiological analyses, and interpreting findings. Previously, at the University of Bari Aldo Moro, I co-supervised a Veterinary Medicine thesis entitled “Bovine Paratuberculosis: An Underestimated Problem?” (2021–2022).
I have also contributed to the evaluation of doctoral research. In September 2024, I served as an expert in the preliminary evaluation of a PhD thesis at the Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha (UCLM), which investigated the spatiotemporal dynamics of Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus transmission and its implications for risk assessment in Iberian ecosystems

title: Teaching, Supervising & & Knowledge Exchange
text:
Professional Training and Knowledge Exchange
My professional training and knowledge exchange activities bridge epidemiological methods, geospatial analysis, and evidence-informed policy.
I presented my work at international discussion forums, including the WHO Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) Community Webinar (2023), and at the EO4Health User Forum (2025), which is the European Space Agency (ESA) Initiatives for Open Innovation and Earth Observation in the aftermath of COVID-19.
As an epidemiologist consultant at Ausvet Europe (now Epimundi) (2022–2023), I delivered hands-on training in scenario tree modelling in R for quantitative epidemiological risk assessment. In June 2022, I co-led a specialist course in Ljubljana, Slovenia, with Angus Cameron (11–16 June), focusing on the quantitative evaluation of surveillance sensitivity for animal infectious diseases. In 2023, I also developed training materials and technical documentation on early-detection surveillance methods to support consistent, practical training in scenario tree modelling.



Scenario tree modelling workshop (Ljubljana,2022)


Earlier, in 2018, as a Technical Support Officer at Avia-GIS, I supported researchers and decision-makers in using VECMAP, a GIS-based decision-support tool for vector-borne disease surveillance and risk assessment. This experience strengthened my ability to explain complex analytical methods, interpret spatial outputs, and translate technical results into information that supports evidence-based decisions.
I also collaborate with universities to share my academic and professional experience with students and early-career researchers, fostering engagement with interdisciplinary research and career development. I delivered a seminar about Policy-Oriented and Exploratory Research for ENZOEM at the University of Córdoba, Spain, in 2025.



ENZOEM seminar, 2025


I collaborate with Oniris VetAgroBio, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine at the University of Nantes, France, to engage with students in the One Health Emerge Master’s programme, as well as veterinary and PhD students.These activities provide opportunities to discuss career pathways in veterinary epidemiology and One Health, highlighting the importance of translating scientific evidence into policy and practice.

Specialist Mentoring in Veterinary Public Health
As a Diplomate of the European College of Veterinary Public Health (ECVPH), I contribute to the development of future specialists through professional mentoring and specialist training. ECVPH Diplomate status recognises advanced expertise in veterinary public health, acquired through structured postgraduate training, demonstrated professional competencies, and a formal examination.
I currently serve as ECVPH residency supervisor for Liliana Martella (2025–2028) and Paolo Capozza (2026–2030), supporting their professional development throughout their specialist training in veterinary public health (Population Medicine). My mentoring approach combines scientific guidance, critical discussion, and support for the development of independent professional judgement, tailored to each resident’s academic and professional background.
Through these activities, I aim to foster a learning environment that connects quantitative methods, epidemiological reasoning, and real-world public health applications, helping students, researchers, and veterinary professionals develop the expertise needed to address emerging infectious diseases and complex One Health challenges.

title: My research at a glance
text:
From 2023 to 2026, I was Principal Investigator of APES (Assessing infectious disease outbreaks with Pandemic and Epidemic riSk) at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC). The project integrated epidemiological, environmental, ecological, agricultural and socioeconomic data to investigate epidemic and pandemic risk and inform health and climate policy.
I developed a global spatial risk model for the WHO-priority zoonotic diseases, including Ebola, Zika and Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever, and an epidemic risk index combining outbreak likelihood with national preparedness and response capacities. The research received international media coverage, including in Carbon Brief, La Repubblica, and Deutschlandfunk.






Risk of the WHO priority diseases, bias adjusted.







geoENV2024 Chania





A companion study assessed leptospirosis risk across Europe, projecting increasing risks under future climate scenarios. The leptospirosis research was disseminated by the JRC and the Instituto de Salud Carlos III.



How leptospirosis cases may change in the future under different climate scenarios. Only meaningful changes are shown.


I also developed an open dataset quantifying heat-related deaths that climate mitigation could avert across 854 European cities by 2050, offering municipal authorities actionable evidence to inform local climate strategies, assess the public health benefits of emissions reductions, and guide policy priorities.

title: My research at a glance
text:
Leveraging epidemic intelligence data
I conceived and developed LLMEpidemic Tracker, an open-source epidemic intelligence prototype developed as part of my Master’s thesis in Big Data, Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (2026). It uses an Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-epi, an open-weight large language model (LLM), to detect and prioritise daily West Nile virus signals from unstructured text, converting them into structured outputs. Local deployment supports data sovereignty, reduces reliance on commercial APIs and streamlines epidemic monitoring.
For the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), I developed a protocol to assess the sensitivity of wildlife disease notification systems. Using capture–recapture methods, I evaluated tularemia reporting in lagomorphs across selected North American and European countries (2014–2019), integrating data from WAHIS, ProMED, PubMed, and news data from the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) to identify potentially undetected disease events.
I also applied Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) to map Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever risk(CCHF), investigating how open-source data can complement conventional surveillance and improve understanding of neglected disease distribution.



The WHO-EIOS system

title: My research at a glance
text:
Disease surveillance and early warning-system
At Ausvet Europe (now Epimundi), I contributed to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance and EU reporting for the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), as well as EFSA’s Bird Flu Radar for early warning of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI).
I also contributed to Transformational Strategies for Farm Output Risk Mitigation (TRANSFORM), a United States Agency for International Development (USAID) funded project, in which I developed livestock health and AMR decision-support tools in Indonesia and Vietnam.
Finally, I applied stochastic scenario-tree models to assess freedom from enzootic bovine leukosis (EBL) through SOUND-control European Cooperation in Science and Technology (COST) Action scientific mission.






Bird Flu Radar

title: My research at a glance
text:
Circular Health research
As a Circular Health Fellow at the University of Florida’s One Health Center of Excellence, I collaborated on interdisciplinary research addressing emerging infectious diseases, veterinary public health, and pandemic preparedness. I carried out research on the risk of African swine fever virus (ASFV) introduction into the United States during the COVID-19 pandemic, advances in thermostable veterinary vaccines, and the potential for SARS-CoV-2 transmission across animal species. This work integrated veterinary, ecological, and biomedical perspectives to inform disease surveillance, vaccine development, and strategies to address emerging infectious disease threats through a One Health approach.



Circular Health by Ilaria Capua

title: My research at a glance
text:
Crimean Congo Haemorragic fever (CCHF)
I earned my PhD in Animal Health and Zoonoses (2019-2022) from the University of Bari, focusing on the risks posed by CCHF to animal and public health. My research combined spatial modelling, environmental data, and risk assessment to investigate the distribution and spread of CCHF across Europe. I identified warmer, drier regions, particularly the Mediterranean basin and areas bordering the Black Sea, as high-risk areas. I also conducted fieldwork in southern Italy, providing evidence of CCHFV circulation in cattle and highlighting the importance of a One Health approach to disease surveillance and prevention.



Hyalomma marginatum, the main vector of Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) in Europe

title: About Me
text:
Angela Fanelli
DVM · MSc One Health · MSc Big Data & AI · ECVPH Diplomate in Population Medicine
I am an epidemiologist specialized in animal and public health, with expertise in big data analytics and data-driven approaches to epidemiological research. My work focuses on integrating advanced statistical modelling, machine learning techniques, and large-scale data processing to strengthen disease early warning systems, improve risk assessment, and support evidence-based decision-making.
